lesson_title: An Egg, a Coat Hanger and a Brick
hook_text: Three things from your kitchen explain every structure on Earth, from a stadium roof to a dam.
clip_script: Squeeze an egg lengthways between your palms. It will not break, because its thin curved shell spreads the push everywhere at once. Tap it on a bowl and it cracks on the spot. That is a shell structure: strength from shape. Car bodies, helmets, domes, the curved roof of the Moses Mabhida Stadium. Now a wire coat hanger: a triangle of thin wire, mostly air, holding a heavy coat. That is a frame: bars joined at corners, strong because of its shape, and above all because of triangles. A square folds sideways; add one diagonal and it locks. Pylons, roof trusses, bicycles, your skeleton, and every cell phone tower. Last, a brick. No skin, no skeleton, just thick heavy clay. That is a solid: strength from mass. Walls, pyramids, the Gariep Dam. Shells are light, frames are tall and open, solids are unmovable. Most things mix them, and now you can see which is which.
visual_style: Whiteboard egg, coat hanger and brick with arrows showing force spreading, triangles locking and mass resisting; three big structures fade in behind them.
mood: Hands-on and surprising, kitchen objects explaining skyscrapers.
pacing: Egg test, hanger test, brick test, each with its big-structure twin, then the three-word summary.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and sort ten objects at home into shell, frame or solid.
